title: Introducing AssemblyAI-STT-3.7 | AssemblyAI
summary: AssemblyAI-STT-3.7 for recorded audio, AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime for live conversation, and AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent for voice agents. 32 languages, live speaker labels that are final at turn end, and the numbers your agent can act on.

## AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent


A caller says "no" and the agent doesn't respond. A caller asks for an appointment time and the agent books the wrong one. At a drive-thru, the kids in the back seat shout an order and the agent takes it. Voice agent builders told us these three problems break more calls than anything else. AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent is built to solve them, at low latency.


### Latency: the final transcript in 86 ms


In a cascaded agent, speech-to-text latency is the time from the caller's last word to the final transcript, plus the time to decide the caller is done. AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent returns the final transcript 86 ms after speech ends. Only 1.0% of words change between partial and final, down from 3.2%, so what the agent acts on early is what it gets at the end. With Gemma 4 31B through AssemblyAI's LLM Gateway and AssemblyAI-TTS-1, end-to-end turn latency is regularly around 250 ms.


Speed against accuracy on voice-agent calls


Lower is better on both axes


Time to final after speech ends from Coval's harness, runs August to November 2026, against pooled normalized word error rate on the same 12,460 voice-agent calls as the charts below. Every provider that reaches the final sooner than AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent makes at least 30% more word errors. Azure and AWS are not shown because Coval reports no time to final for them.


Numbers are where agents fail loudest, and where this model moved most. On 12,460 English voice-agent calls, number errors on Voice Code Bench fall 80% against Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime, so the amount, the account number, and the confirmation code come through. Short replies, the one- and two-word answers that decide a call, are wrong 29% less often and dropped 38% less often. Against the field, entity error on those short utterances is 12.0%, 28% below the next provider, and ahead of Soniox Realtime v6, ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live and Deepgram Nova-3.

Background speech breaks agents outright. The model focuses on the person talking to the agent: words added while the caller was silent fall 47%, so the order comes from the driver, not the back seat. In heavy background noise its word error rate is 5.32%, ahead of Soniox Realtime v6, ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live and Deepgram Nova-3. Background speech suppression works without configuration for most call environments, but for cases where a second talker is close to the microphone we recommend using the near-field voice focus feature.


Two calls in heavy noise. On one, both other providers write a background talker's words as if the caller said them; on the other, both change the e-mail address the caller reads out.

Fewer errors on voice-agent calls


Reduction vs Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime


12,460 English voice-agent calls, paired 95% intervals. Each bar is the percentage reduction in that error on AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent compared with Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime.


Callers who speak English as a second language are where every provider makes the most entity errors. AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent has the lowest rate in every one of the 12 speaker groups we measure. On Indian-accented callers it is 17.6%, ahead of Soniox Realtime v6, ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live and Deepgram Nova-3, and its 5.19% word error rate on Indian-accented English is the lowest of 30 realtime models.

Against the other providers we measured on the same 12,460 calls, with no key terms or context for anyone, AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent has the lowest word error rate, the lowest entity error rate, and the fewest dropped short replies, ahead of Soniox Realtime v6, ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live and Deepgram Nova-3. No other provider has both less background speech and fewer dropped short replies.


Word error rate on voice-agent calls


Lower is better


12,460 English voice-agent calls, normalized word error rate averaged over three noise conditions, every provider through the same harness with no key terms or context, 26 models, runs August to November 2026. AWS Transcribe Streaming and Gladia Solaria are not scored because too many calls failed to return a transcript. Full tables on the[benchmarks page](https://www.assemblyai.com/benchmarks) .


Entity error rate on voice-agent calls


Lower is better


Normalized entity error rate over names, numbers, dates, phone numbers, addresses, emails, codes and technical terms, same calls and runs as above. AWS Transcribe Streaming and Gladia Solaria are not scored because too many calls failed to return a transcript.


Two independent benchmarks ran AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent on their own audio. Voice Arena scores every model on a private conversational set that no vendor can train against, and ranks AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent the #1 streaming model for US English at 2.45% semantic WER, ahead of Fish Transcribe Stream 1 (2.75%) and ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live (2.89%), with Indian English also ahead of Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live. Speko scores streaming models on word error rate, end-of-turn latency, and time to first token at real-time pace, and AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent comes in ahead of ElevenLabs Scribe v3 Live, Deepgram Flux, Soniox Realtime v6, Fish Transcribe Stream 1, and Cartesia Ink-2 on all three.


The price is $0.45/hr, the same as Universal-3.6 Pro Realtime.


Read the full voice-agent benchmark and methodology in the[AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime-Agent research post](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/assemblyai-stt-3-7-realtime-agent-research) .
